paper_title: WeLM-Image: A Unified Image Generation Model towards Visual Intelligence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present \textbf{WeLM-Image}, a unified image foundation model that integrates multimodal understanding into text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and multi-reference synthesis. Designed for single-GPU deployment in WeChat's large-scale consumer applications, the model processes text, reference images, and target latents as one interleaved sequence. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone combines shared attention with independent understanding and generation parameters to limit optimization interference. Equipping each path with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules provides sparse capacity, with 31.7B stored parameters and approximately 5.4B generation parameters activated per target latent token. A generation-oriented data engine combines a knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary with large-scale visual clustering to balance semantic coverage and editing tasks, while training-time evaluation guides iterative data refinement. Bilingual annotations and verified editing supervision support progressive training up to native 1.5K resolution. We optimize generation and editing separately with rubric- and checklist-based rewards, then consolidate the specialized policies through noise-aware on-policy distillation. In the reported overall comparisons, the 1536-resolution model ranks first among the evaluated open-source models on PRISM-Bench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench. MeanFlow-based few-step distillation yields WeLM-Image-Turbo, which generates a $1024\times1024$ image in 4.98\,s on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU using eight guidance-free steps.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Image generation and editing are important steps toward visual intelligence, requiring models to translate language and visual context into coherent, controllable images. Advances in diffusion and flow-based transformers [1, 2] have substantially improved image quality and prompt alignment. As the scope of these models expands, their success increasingly depends on fine-grained control: interpreting long Chinese and English prompts with simultaneous constraints on objects, relations, counts, layout, and style [3]; rendering long Chinese and English text with accurate content and layout [4]; executing complex edits while preserving subject identity [5]; and combining multiple references without confusing their attributes or roles [6]. These requirements motivate common representation in which instructions, reference images, and target latents interact throughout synthesis, allowing multimodal understanding to support fine-grained visual control. Recent image foundation models illustrate different ways to incorporate such understanding into generation. QwenImage [4] uses multimodal language model to condition image synthesis and combines semantic and reconstructive image features for consistent editing. HunyuanImage 3.0 [7] brings language modeling and image generation into shared multimodal backbone, while SenseNova-U1 [8] further explores joint learning directly from pixels and words. Autoregressive language modeling and continuous image generation impose different optimization and capacity requirements. scalable unified model must accommodate these differences while maintaining effective interaction between instructions, reference images, and generated content. For WeChats consumer-facing services, the design must also account for large request volumes and affordable serving costs. We therefore pursue resource eﬀiciency as primary design objective, treating single-GPU deployment and low per-request cost as constraints on model scale and inference design from the outset. Our goal is to maximize overall capability across generation, editing, multi-reference composition, and text rendering within practical parameter and serving budget. This requires joint consideration of model capacity, the growing context of multiple references, and the number of inference steps. To address these modeling and deployment requirements, we present WeLM-Image, unified image foundation model that integrates multimodal understanding into text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and multireference synthesis. All three tasks are expressed as interleaved text and image sequences within one backbone. We adopt dual-path Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) [9, 10] design to give understanding and generation independent parameters, and equip each path with its own Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules [11, 12], forming MoTMoE backbone. In this design, MoT provides specialization across the two objectives to reduce optimization interference; MoE expands capacity within each path through sparse expert activation. Despite this parameter separation, shared attention connects both paths at every layer, allowing target latents to draw jointly on textual instructions, semantic image features, and detailed visual references. With greater active capacity assigned to generation, the model scales to 31.7B stored parameters while activating approximately 5.4B generation parameters per target latent token. We complement the backbone with WeLM-Image-VAE, trained through reconstruction, semantic alignment, and text-oriented decoder fine-tuning to support visual fidelity and text rendering. Building on rotary position embeddings [13] and their multimodal extensions [14], our text-compatible unified three-dimensional rotary positional embedding (3D RoPE) preserves the pretrained language positional transformation while adding spatial structure to image latents. During sampling, conditioning tokens are computed once and cached, so each denoising step recomputes only the noisy target latents (Section 2). To develop these capabilities through training, we organize data construction around semantic coverage, text accuracy, and edit controllability. Starting from curated pool of approximately 0.6B images, knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary makes named concepts retrievable, while large-scale visual clustering organizes coherent appearance patterns. Together, these structures guide semantic rebalancing and task-balanced editing construction. Bilingual captions enriched with OCR information describe visible text and layout; editing pairs are verified against the actual sourcetarget changes, and multi-reference samples bind each input image to the attributes it contributes. Training-time evaluation feeds back into filtering, sampling, task assignment, and mixture ratios to address observed weaknesses. Progressive pretraining couples image-to-text and text-to-image learning in its early stages, then concentrates on generation, editing, and multi-reference tasks as resolution increases. High-resolution continuation and supervised fine-tuning extend the model to native 1.5K generation and complex visual instructions. After supervised fine-tuning, we optimize generation and editing in separate reinforcement-learning branches to address their distinct quality criteria. Generation uses rubric-based prompt alignment [15] alongside aesthetic, textrendering, and visual-naturalness rewards. Editing uses instruction-specific checklists to assess the requested change, content preservation, and visual quality, with instruction following gating the reward. Noise-aware on-policy distillation [16, 17] then consolidates the specialized policies into one model: prompt-enhanced teacher predictions guide global semantics and layout at high noise levels, while standard RL teacher predictions supervise local refinement

sections.title: 2.1 Architecture Overview
sections.content: WeLM-Image is unified model for image creation, instruction-guided editing, and multi-reference generation. Its architecture combines an interleaved multimodal sequence representation with dual-path Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone [9, 10] whose understanding (UND) and generation (GEN) paths each incorporate Mixture-ofExperts (MoE) feed-forward layers [11, 12]. We refer to this architecture as MoTMoE. Understanding tokens (text and image ViT) take the UND path, and generation tokens (clean and noisy image VAE) take the GEN path, while learned routers select experts within the chosen path. Shared attention couples the two paths, which otherwise keep independent projections, normalization, and experts. As illustrated in Figure 2, heterogeneous multimodal inputs are normalized into common interleaved representation. Text and visual elements are independently encoded, projected into model-width token sequences, and serialized in their original semantic order as typed segments within single sequence. Task structure is therefore expressed through token arrangement and attention masks rather than task-specific input pipelines, allowing the same backbone to process all examples through one uniform sequence

sections.title: 2.2 Unified Interleaved Task Representation
sections.content: WeLM-Image is trained jointly on text question answering, visual understanding, text-to-image synthesis, instructionguided editing, and multi-reference generation. Because these tasks differ in schema, sequence length, and image count, task-specific input pipelines are diﬀicult to maintain, and image-resolution bucketing does not yield balanced compute. We therefore adopt unified interleaved task representation in which the model, the packer, and the training losses operate on one ordered multimodal sequence rather than on task-specific formats. This shared interface removes the need for task-specific input pipelines, while packing by total token count balances computation using the complete multimodal sequence rather than image resolution alone. Formally, each sample is serialized as typed text and visual segments that preserve source order, = [S1; S2; . . . ; SK], Sk {text segment, image segment}. (1) Here, is the number of segments, Sk is the k-th segment, and is the resulting source-ordered sequence; semicolons denote segment concatenation. In implementation, text is tokenized with the pretrained language-model tokenizer, while each visual segment is placed as continuous ViT or VAE embeddings. After embedding, all segments share the model hidden width and enter the same backbone. Figure 3 illustrates how this shared interface instantiates two task families. In the generation template, each of the reference images contributes an adjacent clean-VAE segment and ViT segment, which take the GEN path and UND path, respectively. The instruction subsequently takes the UND path, whereas the noisy target VAE takes the GEN path and receives flow-matching supervision. The number of reference images then determines the task instance. Setting = 0 yields text-to-image generation, whereas 1 extends the same template to editing and multi-reference generation. In the understanding template, an optional input-image ViT segment and the question precede the response. All included segments take the UND path, while next-token cross-entropy is applied only to the response. Consequently, omitting the optional ViT segment reduces the same template to pure-text question answering. At training time, these per-sample templates are concatenated into one packed sequence while preserving their segment structure and resetting position indices independently for each sample. Because concatenation would otherwise permit information leakage between samples, the shared-attention mask imposes cross-sample isolation and task-dependent visibility, as described in Section 2.4.

sections.title: 2.3 Visual Encoding
sections.content: To instantiate these interleaved templates, each image segment is represented through two complementary visual encoders. Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder [26, 27] captures high-level content such as objects, spatial relations, layout, and text, while WeLM-Image-VAE maps the image into compact continuous latents that retain the visual details needed for reconstruction and generation. Both representations are projected into backbone tokens and placed in the same interleaved sequence. Reference images therefore provide both content-level guidance and reconstructionlevel visual context, whereas target images are modeled as noisy VAE latents and recovered through flow matching.

sections.title: 2.4 MoT–MoE Backbone
sections.content: MoT and MoE address two distinct requirements. MoT separates understanding and generation into independent parameter paths while retaining joint attention for cross-modal interaction. This separation reduces optimization interference between the two tasks, which differ substantially in their representations and training objectives [9, 10]. However, scaling dense MoT backbone requires widening its feed-forward layers, increasing the parameters and computation activated by every token. MoE offers more eﬀicient way to increase model capacity by adding experts while activating only sparse subset for each token [11,12]. single expert pool shared by understanding and generation would nevertheless weaken the task separation introduced by MoT and could reintroduce interference that hinders convergence. We therefore equip each MoT path with an independent MoE, preserving understandinggeneration decoupling while enabling sparse parameter scaling. The resulting backbone retains standard ViT and VAE interfaces and does not rely on additional timestep-conditioned normalization modules such as AdaLN or AdaLN-Zero [1]. Operationally, the backbone contains 27 decoder layers with hidden size of 2,048. The full multimodal model, including the ViT encoder, stores 31.7B parameters; the independent 83.7M-parameter VAE is excluded. Counts use = 109 and include frozen parameters in stored totals  (Table 2)  . The backbone instantiates this dual-path MoT design in every decoder layer: each layer keeps separate parameters for the UND path and GEN path and couples them through joint attention. The first layer (Layer 0) uses path-specific dense FFN with intermediate size 11,264, whereas Layers 126 replace each dense FFN with path-specific MoE sublayer. MoT therefore supplies the two computation paths of the backbone, while MoE provides sparse conditional capacity inside the feed-forward sublayer of each path. With top-6 expert routing on the UND path and top-20 expert routing on the GEN path, each token on the former activates approximately 2.2B decoder parameters, while each latent token on the latter activates approximately 5.4B parameters in the generation component. During sampling, conditioning tokens are computed once and cached, whereas noisy target latents are recomputed at every denoising step; the 5.4B activated-parameter figure therefore refers to the generation component repeatedly evaluated for each target latent. MoT paths and joint attention. Each token is assigned to fixed path according to its representation type: text and ViT tokens use the UND path, while clean reference and noisy target VAE tokens use the GEN path. At each decoder layer, hidden states are gathered by path and mapped to queries, keys, and values through path-specific pre-attention RMSNorm [37] and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) projections [38]. These tensors are then scattered back to their original sequence positions, and single masked scaled-dot-product attention operation is applied across both paths. Parameter specialization therefore does not partition the attention context. noisy target query on the GEN path, for example, can attend to text and ViT keys/values from the UND path as well as clean reference keys/values from the GEN path. sections.title: 2.5 Text-Compatible Unified 3D RoPE
sections.content: Text and visual tokens share one attention context but require different positional structures. The backbone inherits pretrained one-dimensional RoPE [13]. Visual generation, however, requires intra-image spatial structure that purely sequential index cannot express: patches in the same VAE latent grid often share one packed sequence position, so 1D RoPE does not distinguish height from width. Following multidimensional RoPE designs for multimodal inputs [14], we lift rotary embeddings to single three-axis coordinate system (t, h, w), where is the sequence-axis coordinate and and are the spatial row and column coordinates, and use one rotary operator in each attention layer rather than stacking second spatial encoding on top of the language RoPE. Figure 5 presents the resulting construction from complementary token-coordinate and channel-allocation views. Interleaved axis allocation. Panel (b) of Figure 5 shows the channel-wise mapping. The 64-dimensional rotary subspace of each query and key forms 32 channel pairs. We reuse their original inverse frequencies and assign 12 pairs to and 10 pairs each to and w. These assignments are interleaved across the frequency order rather than grouped into contiguous blocks. This interleaving keeps the range of rotary periods comparable across the three axes. By contrast, grouped split would assign each axis contiguous frequency band and therefore impose systematically different period ranges. This mismatch is particularly harmful when the temporal axis receives the higher-frequency pairs: its shorter periods wrap within long packed prompts, which in our experiments led to gradient-norm spikes and disrupted training. Adding as an anchor keeps the phase at textimage boundaries continuous, while intra-image relative geometry is carried by (h, w). Attention therefore sees single rotary system in which text remains on the original 1D manifold, ViT tokens occupy shared segment index, and VAE latents occupy local 2D neighborhood around that index.

sections.content: Modality-specific supervision. After the unified sequence has passed through the backbone, the resulting hidden states are decoded by separate modality-specific heads. Text states on the UND path are read by the language-model head and trained with autoregressive next-token prediction. Noisy target states on the GEN path are projected into the VAE latent space, where they parameterize flow-matching velocity. Condition tokensinstructions, ViT features, and clean reference latentsenter attention as context and do not receive generation-head supervision. Accordingly, generation supervision is implemented through conditional flow matching [2]. For clean latent z, Gaussian noise ϵ (0, I), and sampled timestep [0, 1], we define the interpolant zt and target velocity as zt = (1 t)z + tϵ, = ϵ z. LFM = ˆvθ v2 2 . (10) Joint objective and loss normalization. Supervised response and CoT positions use standard autoregressive cross entropy LCE. Together with the router regularizer, these two task losses form the joint objective = λCE LCE + λFM LFM + λaux Lrouter. Here, Lrouter is the expert-load regularizer, and λCE, λFM, and λaux weight the text, flow-matching, and router terms, respectively. In the current configuration, these weights are 0.25, 1, and 104. Packed multi-resolution training uses different reduction units for the two primary objectives. The cross-entropy loss is averaged over supervised text tokens, whereas the flow-matching loss is first averaged over all VAE tokens within each target image and then aggregated at the image level. Consequently, 1024 1024 target and 1536 1536 target contribute equally to the flow-matching objective despite containing different numbers of latent tokens. This image-level normalization prevents larger images from receiving greater weight solely because of their resolution and ensures balanced optimization across image areas. sections.title: 3 Data
sections.content: Data plays central role in WeLM-Image. The natural frequency of web-scale image-text pairs is not usable recipe for controllable generation: head concepts dominate the pool, long-tail visual semantics remain under-exposed, and free-form editing construction collapses onto few common operations. Prior work on billion-scale image-text datasets likewise shows that filtering and curation materially determine the value of raw web pool [40, 41]. As shown in Figure 6, we therefore build generation-oriented data engine that reorganizes this pool around what the model must learn to generate, edit, and compose, rather than around becoming general visionlanguage assistant. Specifically, the pipeline first refines noisy web data for quality, retaining curated image pool with aesthetic, resolution, OCR, and safety signals. It then indexes the pool along two complementary structures: knowledge-grounded vocabulary that makes named visual concepts addressable, and large-scale visual clustering that groups images by unnamed but coherent appearance. These two structures supply coverage and balance. On this organized pool we construct text-to-image data, instruction-guided editing and multi-reference generation data, and text-only together with vision-language instruction data, including VQA, that support the prompt interpretation on which generation depends. Finally, training-time evaluation feeds back into filtering, sampling, and mixture ratios, so that data composition remains an active optimization variable rather than fixed recipe.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Infrastructure
sections.content: Storage and Resource Scheduling. The raw data is stored as individual objects in cloud object storage (COS), using bucketed layout that supports cross-region and cross-cluster access without packaging images into large archives. Ray services [42] dynamically schedule heterogeneous GPU and CPU workers, while Pulsar queues decouple storage I/O from data ingestion, cleaning, annotation and quality-control jobs. This computeand message-driven design supports parallel processing and asynchronous result feedback at web scale. Data Indexing. As shown in Figure 7, the processed results are synchronized to three complementary systems. Structured and semi-structured outputs are persistently stored in COS. Textual, vector, attribute, and metadata fields are indexed in Elasticsearch (ES) for sample-level inspection, retrieval, online queries, combined filtering, statistical analysis, and export. Dense annotation features are stored in high-performance feature keyvalue store. datamanagement system built on these services supports dynamic dataset assembly for different training and validation requirements. Targeted subsets with specific quality levels, sources, styles, or vertical domains can typically be selected and exported within half day. The full pipeline sustains more than 15,000 QPS, with selected modules exceeding 100,000 QPS, and has remained stable over multi-month production runs. This shared infrastructure provides the foundation for consistently normalizing and processing heterogeneous data sources.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Data Schema
sections.content: On top of this infrastructure, each raw image-text sample is normalized into unified schema that preserves image identity, source metadata, resolution, aspect ratio, raw text, and storage information. The shared representation gives filtering, annotation, retrieval, and task-construction stages access to the same sample identity and metadata fields, so the same quality-control and attribute-extraction operators can be applied consistently across otherwise heterogeneous sources.

sections.title: 3.1.3 Quality Filtering
sections.content: Pool Refinement. Using this unified representation, we refine raw pool of approximately 5 billion images collected from internal data, Internet data, public datasets, and licensed datasets. The pool is progressively refined through successive quality-control stages. After this process, approximately 0.6 billion images are retained as the curated image pool. Both the resolution and aesthetic statistics in Figure 8 are computed over this filtered 0.6B-image pool. Notably, 59.74% of the retained images fall into the 1024-or-higher resolution groups, providing substantial highresolution foundation for subsequent training-data construction. Quality and Safety. The raw pool is processed by scalable operators for resolution thresholding, blur and clarity assessment, deduplication, and safety filtering, following quality-control dimensions established in large-scale imagetext curation [40, 41]. Low-resolution, blurry, duplicated, unsafe, and otherwise low-quality samples are removed, and pornographic or other sexually explicit NSFW content is excluded before downstream annotation and training. Aesthetic Scoring. For aesthetic quality assessment, we train an internal model inspired by Elo-style pairwise preference modeling, formulation also used to learn preferences among text-to-image outputs [43]. Pairwise human or model judgments are aggregated into relative rankings and distilled into scoring model that captures our internal criteria for visually appealing and trainable images. Figure 8 jointly summarizes the resolution and internal aesthetic distributions of the filtered pool. Most samples are concentrated in the middle aesthetic score ranges, while the continuous score provides flexible signal for constructing mixtures with different quality and coverage requirements. To make the aesthetic score qualitatively interpretable, we organize representative images into four broad score ranges. Figure 9 reserves four examples for each interval, allowing the visual characteristics captured by the aesthetic model to be inspected directly. The filtering operators also act as attribute extractors rather than only as binary gates. Their fine-grained quality, resolution, safety, and content signals are retained for downstream sampling, routing, mixture construction, and distribution diagnosis.

sections.title: 3.2 Coverage and Balance
sections.content: After refinement and reusable annotation, we organize the curated pool along two complementary axes. The knowledgegrounded vocabulary makes named visual concepts explicitly addressable, while visual clustering captures coherent appearance patterns that may not yet have stable semantic name. The two structures are maintained as loop rather than as independent indexes: unnamed visual groups expose coverage gaps that can expand the vocabulary, and named concepts supply the semantic targets against which the clustered pool is retrieved and rebalanced.

sections.title: 3.2.1 Visual Vocabulary
sections.content: Concept Selection. To improve semantic coverage beyond the natural frequency of web data, we construct knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary from both open and internal sources. We start from open lexical resources such as Cilin [44] and filter them together with an internal WeChat Knowledge Graph (KG), retaining concepts that are visually meaningful for image generation. The resulting vocabulary contains both entities and attributes, covering objects, people, scenes, styles, materials, actions, relations, and other visually grounded concepts. Concept Cleaning. During vocabulary construction, we preserve the entity / attribute distinction while applying extensive cleaning to improve concept purity. LLM-based checks remove abstract, ambiguous, non-visual, or noisy items. We further use Qwen3-embedding [45] plus reranking pipeline to retrieve and verify near-synonyms, aliases, and visually similar expressions, allowing fragmented surface forms to be merged into cleaner concept nodes. This process turns flat word list into structured topology of concepts, synonym relations, and parent-child relations rather than collection of isolated terms. Concept Hierarchy. To reduce the singularity of individual words, we build complete hierarchical structure for the vocabulary. Each concept is placed in broader semantic context, with upper-level categories supporting distribution analysis and lower-level nodes preserving fine-grained visual distinctions. Query Expansion. To quickly supplement data for any concept, we expand retrieval queries with aliases, descriptive phrases, visual keywords, and search-oriented expressions. The resulting vocabulary makes long-tail concepts addressable, retrievable, sampleable, and evaluable. As shown in Figure 10, each final node connects ontology, retrieval, and synonym knowledge in one structured representation.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Visual Clustering
sections.content: Image Embeddings. In parallel with the knowledge vocabulary, we build large-scale visual embedding space over the image pool. Images are encoded with Qwen3-VL-Embedding [45], and masks derived from filtering signals such as aesthetic scores select high-quality subsets for downstream clustering and analysis. Hierarchical Clustering. We apply balanced hierarchical variant of spherical k-means [46] to cluster hundreds of millions of images into large number of visually coherent groups. The resulting hierarchy provides structured coverage map over the image distribution. Joint Coverage. Clustering is not used merely for indexing or compression. Together with the knowledge vocabulary, it organizes the same pool along complementary axes. The vocabulary makes named concepts addressable, retrievable, and quota-sampleable, so text-to-image construction can ground images in explicit semantic targets rather than in raw web frequency, as detailed in Section 3.3.1. Clusters provide the visual counterpart: they map unnamed but coherent appearance, make coverage gaps inspectable, and serve as routing units for downstream generation and editing. Representative images from each cluster can be classified by VLM to estimate task suitability, which reduces the instability of per-image free-form construction and lets sampling and assignment operate on visually coherent groups rather than isolated samples. Patterns that the vocabulary does not yet name become candidates for concept expansion, query refinement, and targeted supplementation, feeding newly discovered visual regularities back into the semantic scaffold. Coverage therefore comes from making both named semantics and unnamed appearance addressable, while balance comes from reweighting long-tail concepts through the vocabulary and routing visually coherent groups through clusters instead of sampling by natural frequency.

sections.title: 3.3 Task Data
sections.content: The semantic vocabulary and visual clusters turn the curated pool into an organized source from which task-specific supervision can be constructed. We use this common foundation to build text-to-image, instruction-guided editing, multi-reference generation, and understanding-oriented datasets with task-appropriate sampling and verification.

sections.title: 3.3.1 Text-to-Image
sections.content: Semantic Sampling and Rebalancing. Building on the complementary semantic and visual organization introduced in Section 3.2, we use the KG vocabulary from Section 3.2.1 to define explicit semantic targets for text-to-image pretraining. Each KG node is encoded into retrieval representation, and concept-to-image retrieval is used to recall candidate images from the large-scale image pool. To improve semantic precision, we further apply image-toconcept reverse verification: candidate images are matched back against the target concept vocabulary, and images with bidirectional semantic agreement are prioritized. To convert this semantic coverage into balanced training set, we assign per-concept quotas and select globally unique images for each KG word instead of sampling purely according to raw web frequency. This reduces repeated exposure to frequent concepts and gives long-tail entities and attributes greater training visibility. The resulting KG matching statistics, together with the cluster-side coverage map from Section 3.2.2, reveal which named concepts or coherent visual regions remain missing or under-covered. For these gaps, we use the expanded queries associated with each vocabulary node to retrieve and supplement additional data, prioritizing preferred sources when available and using fallback sources to maintain scale. This stage outputs sampled training rows, per-word statistics, unsatisfied concepts, and summary files, making it possible to distinguish well-covered concepts from those still limited by the underlying pool. Text-to-image data is therefore organized around semantic coverage and balance rather than raw frequency. Caption Construction. The sampled images are paired with captions designed along multiple axes, including language, length, semantic granularity, and style awareness. Randomized bilingual templates diversify their surface form across neutral descriptions, concise user-like expressions, and generation-style prompts while preserving the same underlying visual semantics. This design follows evidence that recaptioning noisy web pairs with richer synthetic descriptions can substantially improve prompt following [47]. For text-heavy images, posters, documents, UI screenshots, and other special layouts, later rewrite stage incorporates the reusable OCR and watermark signals from Section 3.1.4. Captions are produced at different levels of detail so that visible text, layout, and ordinary visual content can be described faithfully without forcing every sample into maximal description.

sections.title: 3.3.2 Image Editing
sections.content: Task-Balanced Assignment. Image editing data is constructed around structured editing ontology. We define editing tasks using hierarchy of coarseand fine-grained categories, including object addition, object removal, background replacement, local attribute modification, portrait editing, product editing, restoration, and reasoningoriented edits. Recent general-purpose editing datasets and systems similarly organize supervision by operation type [5, 24, 48]. key challenge is that free-form editing instruction generation naturally produces long-tailed task distribution. Common operations such as removal, addition, background replacement, and global stylization tend to dominate, while more specific editing categories receive far fewer samples. To address this, we control task balance earlier, at the cluster assignment and sample selection stage, rather than relying on the prompt generator to choose tasks opportunistically. We first classify visual clusters with VLM, which predicts strong and possible editing-task aﬀinities from representative images. These aﬀinities form candidate pool for balanced cluster-to-task assignment algorithm that jointly considers task balance and visual suitability. Images sampled from the assigned clusters carry fixed edit tag, as shown in Figure 11, which acts as hard prior so that instruction generation follows the assigned task rather than selecting an operation opportunistically. Pair Construction. After clusters are assigned to editing tasks, we construct editing pairs from two complementary sources. First, within visually coherent cluster, we mine real-image pairs that share common transformation patterns, such as portrait changes, object changes, or viewpoint changes. Inspired by the graphical representation used in ZImage [49], we treat an image and its related variants as small graph. Pairwise combinations can expand the number of training pairs, create mixed-editing supervision, and produce useful inverse pairs. This turns cluster-level visual regularities into reusable editing supervision instead of relying only on independent free-form generation. Second, we decompose editing tasks into vertical categories and use different expert models for object-level, backgroundlevel, portrait-level, product-level, restoration, and reasoning-oriented edits. For many tasks, we construct pairs in reverse direction: the target image is kept as real image from the data pool, and the corresponding source image and instruction are derived around it. This reduces synthetic target artifacts and keeps the final target distribution grounded in real images. Verification and Prompt Diversification. All constructed pairs pass through VLM-based quality gate. The checker verifies whether the source-target difference is valid, detects no-change cases, and fixes instructions that miss or misdescribe edit points.

sections.content: Finally, we use the verified differences and refined instruction as the factual basis for prompt diversification. The same verified edit is rewritten into multiple semantically equivalent user prompts, covering concise commands, tag-like prompts, long narrative descriptions, spoken-style instructions, and noisy user-like phrasing. In this way, task-aware cluster assignment controls task balance, expert construction provides diverse pair sources, VLM checking guarantees correctness, and difference-grounded rewriting exposes the model to realistic user expressions while reducing semantic drift.

sections.title: 3.3.3 Multi-Reference
sections.content: Construction Paths. Single-image editing pairs cannot capture requests that require cross-image consistency, such as preserving identity while transferring garment, product, scene, or style from another image. Prior unified generators have likewise shown that mixed imagetext conditioning can express subject-driven and visual-conditional generation tasks [6]. We therefore construct samples containing two to four source or reference images, an instruction grounded in their content, and one target image through two complementary paths. The reverse path retains real target from the curated pool and derives suitable references and an instruction around it, reducing synthetic-target artifacts. The forward path instead assembles real source images and synthesizes the target with multi-reference image editor. Role-Aware Assembly. Each source is assigned role, such as identity, garment, object, scene, style, or layout reference. Combinations of these roles define 18 tasks, including co-shoot, virtual try-on, product placement, and reference-guided relighting, together with constraints on source diversity and compatibility. For the forward path, VLM annotates cluster representatives to form an entity pool of approximately 750,000 images, and quota-based assembler selects compatible but visually diverse source combinations from the embedding space. Hard constraints remove invalid combinations before VLM writes an instruction that explicitly binds each Image to the attributes to preserve or change, after which the editor synthesizes the target. Verification and Prompt Diversification. VLM checker verifies reference roles, removes irrelevant inputs, renumbers image indices, and corrects inconsistent instructions. We retain facial and subject similarity, CLIP alignment [50], OCR, and aesthetic scores for diagnosis, but controlled corruption study showed that thresholding these metrics rejects many valid samples, whereas VLM judge detects nearly all introduced failures with low falserejection rate. Production filtering therefore enforces resolution and deduplication requirements, rejects source-target copies, and requires positive VLM usability verdict; the remaining metrics are advisory. The verified differences and roles then support semantically equivalent prompt rewrites with varied lengths and styles while preserving the contribution of each reference. The resulting dataset contains several hundred thousand examples across the 18 tasks.

sections.title: 3.3.4 Understanding Data
sections.content: WeLM-Image is designed around unified model architecture. The current version still focuses primarily on image generation and image editing, but we believe the unified formulation has greater long-term potential. Adding understanding-oriented data can directly improve the models ability to interpret prompts, reason over visual semantics, and produce better images. Text Data. We incorporate proportion of text-only data to preserve the models general language capabilities and its ability to interpret complex textual instructions. VLM Instructions. The current version primarily relies on open-source vision-language datasets, such as LLaVAOneVision-1.5-Instruct [51], FineVision [52], and Honey-15M [53], together with proprietary captioning data. After dataset-level deduplication, cleaning, quality filtering, and training-recipe optimization, these sources are assembled into the vision-language instruction dataset. Task Taxonomy. We establish unified labeling taxonomy covering General VQA, Caption & Knowledge, Chart, OCR, Document, Grounding, Code, Math, Table, Science, Counting, GUI, Medical, Spatial, and Egocentric tasks. The filtering pipeline removes repetitive text, low-quality images, and images with extreme aspect ratios while mitigating language mixing and other sources of noise. Together, these procedures improve the quality, consistency, and diversity of understanding-oriented supervision. Reverse Alignment. In addition to curated text-only and vision-language data, large amount of text-to-image data can naturally become vision-language alignment data after reverse construction. By treating generated or retrieved images as visual inputs and deriving corresponding descriptions, judgments, or instructions, the same data pool can support both generation training and image-text understanding, consistent with recent unified multimodal pretraining studies [10, 54]. In the next version, we plan to further explore improvements to the models visual understanding capability while keeping generation and editing as the main application targets.

sections.title: 3.4 Training Mixtures and Feedback
sections.content: After construction and task-specific verification within each data pipeline, the retained data is assembled into stagedependent training mixtures and continually updated using feedback from model evaluation.

sections.title: 3.4.1 Stage-Wise Mixtures
sections.content: The verified and rebalanced data is assembled according to the capability contributed by each source. High-quality text-to-image samples provide broad visual coverage, KG-guided samples improve long-tail semantic exposure, editing and multi-reference data strengthen controllable and compositional generation, and text-only and vision-language supervision improve prompt understanding and visual semantic parsing. Mixture ratios are scheduled by training stage rather than held fixed throughout the pipeline. Early pretraining retains understanding-oriented data to establish the shared multimodal interface, whereas high-resolution continuation and SFT concentrate the budget on text-to-image, editing, and multi-reference generation, as detailed in Table 3.

sections.title: 3.4.2 Feedback Loop
sections.content: Data construction is treated as training-time feedback loop rather than one-shot filtering pipeline. Evaluations run throughout training to reveal data issues, capability regressions, semantic coverage gaps, and task-distribution biases. The resulting diagnostics are returned to the data engine to adjust filtering thresholds, retrieval queries, sampling quotas, task assignments, and mixture ratios, connecting observed model weaknesses to the stage of data construction that can address them. As new weaknesses emerge, the verified mixture is updated for the next training iteration, so data composition remains an active optimization variable rather than fixed recipe. Overall, filtering, knowledgeand cluster-based rebalancing, task-specific construction, and training-time feedback are successive stages of the same generation-oriented objective: turning web-scale data into mixture from which controllable generation can actually be learned.

sections.title: 4 Training
sections.content: WeLM-Image is trained as one pipeline from progressive pretraining through instruction SFT, task-separated reinforcement learning, and two distillation stages, as shown in Figure 12. Pretraining and SFT install the dual-path backbone and raise resolution. T2I RL and I2I RL then align generation and editing separately. On-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates the resulting policies, and Meanflow-based distillation shortens the sampling trajectory for deployment. Table 3 records the pretraining and SFT recipe.

sections.title: 4.1 Initialization
sections.content: Both paths of the dual-path backbone are initialized from the same pretrained Kimi-VL [27] languagevision checkpoint. Token embeddings and the language-model head are loaded once and shared across the two paths. For every transformer layer, the understanding-path MLA projections, LayerNorms, and feed-forward weightsincluding the dense first layer and the full MoE of routed experts, shared experts, and the routerare taken from Kimi-VL, then replicated onto the generation path so that both paths start from the same pretrained snapshot. The final RMSNorm is copied in the same way. The ViT and its multimodal projector are loaded from the same checkpoint. Only the generation-specific VAE bridges and the timestep embedder start from random initialization.

sections.title: 4.3 Post-training
sections.content: After SFT, we optimize text-to-image generation (T2I) and image-to-image editing (I2I) as two separate reinforcementlearning branches initialized from the same checkpoint, with independent training data, rewards, rollouts, and LoRA adapters [56]. In both branches, the pretrained backbone stays frozen and training updates only generation-side LoRA modules. In generation attention, LoRA is applied to the query, keyvalue, and output projections. In the dense and shared-expert feed-forward networks, it is applied to the gate, up, and down projections. The routed generation experts receive LoRA on the fused gateup and down projections. Our ablations on the adapter scope show that jointly applying LoRA to the MoE layers consistently improves performance for both T2I generation and image editing. The understanding pathway, embeddings, normalization layers, and MoE router remain frozen. Each branch is optimized with DiffusionNFT [57], which converts reward-scored rollouts from an EMA policy into optimality supervision for forward-process objective over implicit positive and negative velocity fields. After the two RL branches converge, on-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates their capabilities into single student checkpoint, eliminating the need to switch between separate T2I and I2I adapters at inference and preparing the merged policy for subsequent deployment distillation.

sections.title: 4.3.1 Text-to-Image Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: For text-to-image generation, four independently trained VLM rewards measure image-text alignment, aesthetics, text rendering, and visual naturalness. We use GDPO [58] to normalize the heterogeneous reward dimensions separately within each rollout group before aggregation. Image-text alignment reward. Rather than regressing single opaque alignment score, we adopt rubric-based reward in the spirit of RubricRL [15]. Before rollout, each training prompt is decomposed into structured rubric, that is, set of atomic and visually verifiable criteria, and the reward is obtained by judging the candidate image against these criteria and aggregating the item-level outcomes. Rubric construction is deliberately image-blind, and the resulting rubric is reused for every rollout of the prompt, so that all candidates within group are scored under an identical standard. Rubric generation is anchored on curated criterion pool rather than produced free-form. The pool is organized around the dimensions of imagetext consistency that matter in practice, including object presence and count, rendered text, attributes, spatial relations, actions, negation, and style or layout constraints. Given prompt, the generator identifies the most relevant dimensions, instantiates criteria accordingly, applies prompt-adaptive weighting that emphasizes the salient dimensions, and caps the total number of criteria per prompt. Each prompt and each criterion carries dimension tag. Because the entire construction pipeline runs offline, these tags enable category-aware sampling and allow us to systematically resample the offline training corpus toward failure modes observed in the current model. Since pass rates are tracked separately per dimension, gains in frequent categories cannot mask persistent failures in long-tail ones. During RL training, we present all rollouts of the same prompt to the judge as group rather than scoring each candidate independently. Group-wise scoring provides shared comparison context, reduces cross-call calibration variance, and makes fine-grained differences in rubric satisfaction easier to distinguish. The judge returns an itemlevel decision with supporting evidence for every criterion and rollout, and we aggregate these decisions according to item assessability and importance. This itemized formulation yields both scalar training signal and fine-grained failure diagnosis. Aesthetic reward. We first train pairwise VLM to compare two same-prompt images in terms of composition, lighting, color harmony, texture, and overall visual appeal. Unlike scalar preference models such as PickScore, which learn single score from pairwise choices [43], our pairwise model learns from structured comparison supervision comprising the preference verdict, visual evidence, per-image dimension scores, and dimension-importance weights. We then apply this teacher to multiple same-prompt opponents and aggregate its pairwise outputs into stable absolute target for each image. Distilling these multi-opponent targets into pointwise reward model preserves the reliability and interpretability of comparative reasoning while allowing each rollout image to be scored independently with single forward pass during RL. As dedicated component of the aesthetic reward, we additionally train visual-deformation detector. Generalpurpose VLMs remain relatively weak at recognizing malformed structures directly. We find, however, that conditioning VLM on the candidate image together with coarse deformation category elicits high-confidence chain-ofthought rationales that localize and explain the corresponding defect. These category-conditioned rationales provide dense supervision beyond the original coarse labels, allowing us to train an accurate deformation reward model with only modest amount of annotated data. Text-rendering reward. All prompts are pre-annotated according to whether rendered text may reasonably appear

sections.content: in the image. Under an elastic text constraint, rendered text is optional: if text appears, the evaluator checks whether it is semantically incorrect, structurally anomalous, illegible, or composed of pseudo-characters, while correct and legible text incurs no penalty. If prompt is labeled as incompatible with rendered text, any visible text is penalized. Because open-source VLMs remain relatively weak at perceiving fine-grained glyph-level structural anomalies, particularly in rendered Chinese characters, we train dedicated structural-anomaly perception model. It robustly detects glyph deformation, missing or redundant strokes, blurriness, and misalignment in both Chinese and English across challenging settings, including dense text, small text, rare Chinese characters, and artistic typography. The resulting structured judgments are aggregated into the text-rendering reward. Visual-naturalness reward. The fourth VLM directly evaluates visual naturalness, focusing on recognizable syntheticimage cues such as plastic or over-smoothed textures, repeated micro-patterns, incoherent local details, and implausibly uniform lighting. This reward encourages natural textures, coherent local details, and physically plausible illumination. Prompt curation and category-aware reward routing. We construct the T2I RL prompt pool with balanced sampling across semantic categories and short-, medium-, and long-form prompts. Before online training, we perform offline rollouts with the base policy and estimate the mean and variance of the composite reward for each prompt. We retain prompts whose mean reward lies within target range and whose reward variance exceeds predefined threshold. This removes prompts that are either already solved or consistently fail across rollouts, concentrating RL updates on learnable cases that provide informative within-group contrasts. We further assign each prompt one or more category labels and use them to determine its reward-weight vector offline. For example, typography prompts place greater emphasis on text rendering, whereas portrait prompts assign more weight to aesthetic and deformationrelated signals. This offline routing aligns the optimization objective with the quality requirements of each category while avoiding single reward dimension dominating the heterogeneous training mixture. Mixed original/PE rollout groups. Prompt enhancement (PE) is applied inside the rollout group rather than as separate training stream. For every canonical prompt, part of the group is generated from the original prompt and the remainder from its semantically constrained enhanced form. Mixing the two prompt forms in one relative group broadens visual coverage, increases within-group reward variance, and provides more informative positive and negative samples than repeatedly sampling only one formulation.

sections.title: 4.3.2 Image Editing Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: Training data and action balancing. We categorize image editing instructions into 27 editing action types and use this taxonomy to filter the training data. First, we use multiple open-source reward models to evaluate and rank the diﬀiculty of the instructions offline. During instruction sampling, we set the target ratio of easy, medium, and hard samples to 3 : 5 : 2. Within each editing action category, we further exclude samples at the extremes of the diﬀiculty spectrum, including those with near-zero success rates (excessively diﬀicult) and those with near-saturated success rates (overly easy). This filtering retains more informative samples that provide stronger learning signals for policy optimization. Checklist-based editing reward. We propose category-aware, hierarchical checklist-based reward for evaluating image editing. Before training, an offline checklist generator built on VLM constructs an instruction-specific evaluation checklist. The generator conditions on the corresponding action label as task-level context, enabling it to define evaluation dimensions and criteria tailored to the specific editing category. During training, each instruction consistently reuses its precomputed checklist, ensuring consistent reward evaluation. Each checklist covers three dimensions: prompt following, consistency, and visual quality. The VLM-based evaluator assigns each criterion status oi {pass, fail, not-assessable} for each candidate edited image. Failed criteria additionally receive mild, medium, or severe failure level. Within each dimension, failed criteria incur penalties determined jointly by criterion importance and failure severity. We subtract the accumulated penalties from fixed score budget and normalize the result to obtain rP , rC, rQ [0, 1] for prompt following, consistency, and visual quality, respectively. Pass and not-assessable outcomes incur no penalty. We use prompt following as multiplicative gate: redit = rP (0.4 + 0.4rC + 0.2rQ) . (12) This prevents high consistency or visual quality from compensating for failure to perform the editing instruction. Editing-specific training strategies. We use moderate classifier-free guidance (CFG) [25] to rollout samples while excluding the unconditional branch from the training objective, thereby improving the reliability of rewards and training stability. To accelerate sampling, we use half the standard number of inference steps during rollout, while retaining the complete trajectories for training. In contrast to RL for T2I task, we find that training on complete trajectories yields improved performance for image editing tasks.

sections.title: 4.3.3 On-policy Distillation
sections.content: Applying RL independently to T2I task and image editing task yields strong task-specific experts (Teacher), while training on mixed-task data provides balanced generalization but may not reach the performance ceiling of each domain. We therefore employ On-policy Distillation (OPD) [16, 17] to integrate the specialized capabilities of the two experts into unified model. We initialize the student model from an SFT checkpoint. During rollout, we employ CFG sampling to generate and record the students denoising trajectories. During training, the intermediate states along each trajectory are routed to the corresponding T2I or image-editing RL teacher according to the task category of each sample. Our supervision objective aligns both the students positive predictions and its conditional guidance directions with those produced by the corresponding teacher. To further enhance the models semantic and structural planning capabilities, we introduce PE teacher in addition to the RL teacher and propose noise-aware OPD. This mechanism selects the supervision target according to the learning requirements at different stages of the denoising process. At high noise levels, the objective derived from the PE teacher guides the student in learning global semantics and content layout. At low noise levels, we retain the standard RL teacher to refine local attributes and visual quality. Let {T2I, Edit} denote the task and vTq (xt, t, c) the conditional velocity predicted by the corresponding teacher. The noise-aware target is (cid:3) (cid:2) bvTq (xt, t, c) = vTq (xt, t, c) + ht vTq (xt, t, cPE) vTq (xt, t, c) , (13) where ht = 1 at high noise levels and ht = 0 at low noise levels, and and cPE denote the original condition and its semantically constrained prompt-enhanced version, respectively.

sections.title: 4.3.4 Few-step Distillation
sections.content: To improve inference eﬀiciency, we introduce scalable few-step distillation framework based on the average-velocity formulation of MeanFlow [18] in the final training stage. It compresses full-step model with CFG into guidancefree 8/4 step model. By transferring the teachers long-trajectory generative capability to fixed few-step schedule and optimizing the students global transport behavior under large sampling steps, our framework preserves prompt adherence, global composition, and visual fidelity while substantially accelerating inference. Our framework combines average-velocity MeanFlow consistency distillation with DMD-style online trajectory alignment [59]. Given clean latent predicted by the student, an auxiliary predictor and the teacher independently estimate the mean flow over the same noise interval. Their discrepancy quantifies the transport gap between the teacher and student trajectories and serves as the optimization signal for the student. To align training with the 8/4-step sampler, we introduce local trajectory anchoring. For each interval sampled from the inference schedule, fine-grained teacher integration provides target mean flow that directly supervises the students initial velocity. Complementing random-interval alignment, this objective reduces Euler discretization errors and mitigates structural drift, texture loss, and detail degradation. Together, these objectives enable eﬀicient few-step generation while preserving text rendering, semantic understanding, composition, and visual fidelity.

sections.title: 4.4 Training Infrastructure
sections.content: The unified interface of WeLM-Image also simplifies its training infrastructure. Understanding, text-to-image generation, editing, and multi-reference synthesis are all represented as interleaved sequences of text tokens, semantic image tokens, and image latent tokens. Position IDs, attention masks, and loss masks describe the structure and supervision of each example. Although text and image targets use different objectives, the tasks share one Transformer training loop. Multi-task training therefore becomes sequence-training problem that can reuse mature LLM infrastructure. We apply several established LLM training techniques to this shared interface. Token packing [19] combines variablelength examples within common token budget, reducing padding while keeping examples separate through attention masks. Fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) [20] distributes parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across accelerators to reduce memory use per device. For high-resolution and multi-reference training, Ulysses context parallelism (CP) [21] splits long sequence across devices while preserving attention within each example, supporting packed contexts of up to 64K tokens. BF16 mixed precision and activation checkpointing further reduce memory requirements. The MoE backbone also offers natural path to expert parallelism (EP), which distributes experts across devices and sends tokens to their selected experts. The reported training recipe uses FSDP and CP, with EP size set to 1  (Table 3)  . These choices can be made at the training system level while retaining the same multi-task input interface.

sections.content: Inference cost determines whether unified generation-and-editing model can be deployed at scale. Editing is the critical case because the visual context grows with the number of input images, and attention over the concatenated token sequence can make latency grow super-linearly. We therefore measure end-to-end latency on text-to-image generation and on instruction-guided editing with one to four input images, treating single-image editing and multi-reference composition as one family parameterized by the number of inputs. Table 4 compares the end-to-end inference latency of WeLM-Image against popular models. Protocol. All measurements use NVIDIA H20 GPUs, fixed random seed, and an identical software stack (PyTorch 2.9.1, Diffusers 0.39.0, Transformers 5.2.0). Each configuration is served on single GPU, except HunyuanImage3.0-Instruct-Distil, which requires 4-way tensor-parallel instance spanning four GPUs. For every modelcase pair we execute one warm-up pass followed by three timed passes, and report the mean wall-clock time from the prompt and reference images to the decoded output, excluding model loading. Run-to-run variation is negligible, staying below 0.5% of the mean throughout. We evaluate WeLM-Image at 50 sampling steps and its distilled variant WeLM-Image-Turbo at 8 steps. The baselines include Qwen-Image-2512 and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, each in its released standard setting and with its oﬀicial 4step Lightning LoRA. We also include Z-Image, SenseNova-U1-8B-MoT, and HunyuanImage-3.0-Instruct-Distil. The latter, like our models and SenseNova-U1-8B-MoT, serves both generation and editing from one checkpoint. One sampling detail is important when reading the table. The Lightning configurations and WeLM-Image-Turbo are guidance-free (true_cfg_scale= 1) and evaluate the network once per step, whereas the standard configurations use classifier-free guidance and evaluate it twice. Step counts alone therefore understate the compute gap between the two regimes by factor of two. Because the systems also differ in size, sampling schedule, and model parallelism, these results characterize the released inference settings rather than isolating architectural eﬀiciency. Our models run through PyTorch scaled dot-product attention without kernel-level acceleration, quantization, step caching, or graph compilation, so their figures are an unoptimized upper bound. Text-to-image latency. At matched 50-step budget, WeLM-Image is consistently faster than Qwen-Image-2512, and its margin widens with resolution, from 8% at 1024 576 to 15% at 1024 1024. The difference reflects their scaling behaviour. Over this range, the pixel count grows by 1.78 while the latency of WeLM-Image grows by only 1.73, against 1.87 for Qwen-Image-2512 and 1.85 for Z-Image. Cost is thus close to linear in the number of generated tokens, indicating that quadratic attention has not yet become the dominant term at megapixel resolution. It also depends on the token count rather than the spatial layout. Transposed portrait resolutions differ from their landscape counterparts by at most 0.3%, and we omit them from the table. With one input image WeLM-Image is 1.96 faster than Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 despite using more sampling steps (50 versus 40), and the gap widens to 5.10 with four inputs. sections.title: 6.1.1 Text-to-Image & Text Rendering
sections.content: To evaluate the foundational generation quality and the specific capability of rendering complex visual text, we benchmark WeLM-Image against suite of leading open-source and proprietary text-to-image models, including QwenImage [4], Qwen-Image-2512 [4], Z-Image-Turbo [49], HunyuanImage-3.0 [7], ERNIE-Image-Turbo [60], GLMImage [61], HiDream-O1-Image [62], SenseNova-U1-8B-MoT [8], Boogu-Image-0.1 [54] and FLUX.2-dev [63]. We report results on multiple widely-used benchmarks: GenEval [64], PRISM-Bench [22], OneIG-Bench [65], TIIF-Bench [3], DPG-Bench [66], Qwen-Image-Bench [23], WeGenBench [67], LongText-Bench [68], and CVTG2K [69], which together cover compositional generation, long/complex text rendering, general image quality, and instruction-following ability. Table 5 summarizes the overall quantitative results. We can see that WeLM-Image ranks among the top-tier open-source models on both mainstream and emerging evaluation benchmarks. GenEval GenEval [64] is designed to rigorously evaluate object-centric generation capabilities. Unlike benchmarks that rely on holistic image-text alignment scores, GenEval isolates specific compositional skills. It tests whether model can accurately render single or multiple distinct objects, correctly bind attributes (e.g., colors) to specific entities, adhere to precise object counts, and understand complex spatial relations (e.g., left of, below). This fine-grained evaluation is crucial for determining if model truly understands object composition rather than merely memorizing co-occurrences. Table 6 shows that the WeLM-Image family performs strongly on GenEval: WeLM-Image-Turbo-8step achieves perfect score (tied for first) on single-object generation, while WeLM-Image attains the second-highest score on single-object generation and ranks third on attribute binding among open-source models, reflecting reliable compositional understanding and competitive object-level fidelity. PRISM-Bench PRISM-Bench [22] is comprehensive VLM-powered benchmark that goes beyond simple textimage matching. It evaluates models across diverse axes including Imagination (creative interpretation of abstract concepts), Entity (accurate rendering of specific subjects), Style (adherence to requested artistic mediums), and Composition (overall visual layout). By leveraging advanced Vision-Language Models as evaluators, PRISM-Bench offers holistic assessment that jointly considers the logical reasoning behind the prompt and the aesthetic quality of the generated image. As shown in Table 7, WeLM-Image ranks first among open-source models in Overall score as well as across Imagination, Style, and Composition, while placing third in Entity (with WeLM-Image-Turbo8step also ranking second in Style and third in Overall), demonstrating strong and well-rounded performance across PRISM-Benchs fine-grained dimensions.

Table 17 shows that the WeLM-Image family achieves top-three open-source performance on six ImgEdit subtasks and ranks third on the overall score. Notably, WeLM-Image-Turbo-8step leads Background, Replace, and Style, while WeLM-Image attains the best Add and Compose scores, demonstrating strong coverage across diverse editing operations. UnicBench UnicBench [24] is comprehensive image-editing benchmark covering 1,100 manually reviewed test cases across 22 sub-tasks spanning four major categories: Object, Attribute, Scene, and Reasoning Editing. Beyond conventional evaluation, it introduces Non-edit Consistency and Reasoning Accuracy metrics to enable fine-grained diagnosis of both basic and complex, reasoning-driven editing capabilities. Table 18 highlights that WeLM-Image ranks first among open-source models across all UnicBench metrics. Together with WeLM-Image-Turbo-8step placing second on NC and third on both VQ and Overall, the WeLM-Image family shows strong instruction alignment and visual quality. WeGenEditBench Although public benchmarks provide broad comparisons, they remain limited in their coverage of long instructions, compositional editing goals, fine-grained text modification, and multi-reference image composition. Their VLM-based evaluators also commonly assess an edited image holistically without explicit sample-specific verification criteria, allowing salient successful edit or high overall visual quality to obscure omitted operations, unintended modifications, or incorrect reference binding. To address these limitations, we construct WeGenEditBench, comprising 2,740 manually collected and curated samples. It contains 1,008 single-image editing samples covering local manipulation, portrait and aesthetic editing, and reasoning-intensive editing. The benchmark further includes 1,000 text editing samples covering textual-content modification, text-style adjustment, and complex visual layouts, together with 732 multi-image editing samples designed to evaluate identity and product references, style transfer, and multi-reference composition. For each sample, we generate and freeze fine-grained checklist before evaluating model outputs. Complex instructions are decomposed into independently verifiable requirements specifying the editing target, operation, attribute, location, and expected change. These requirements are organized into four dimensions: Edit Goal (EG), Preservation (PR), Visual Quality (VQ), and Domain-specific Capability (DS). fixed VLM judge provides an explicit rationale and deduction for every checklist item before assigning the dimensional scores. All models are evaluated using identical pre-generated checklists, ensuring consistent and traceable evaluation criteria.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We have presented WeLM-Image, unified image foundation model that brings multimodal understanding into textto-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and multi-reference synthesis. Its MoTMoE backbone combines specialized understanding and generation parameters with shared attention, allowing textual instructions and visual references to guide synthesis throughout the model. Sparse expert activation, dedicated VAE, and text-compatible spatial encoding provide the capacity and visual representation needed for detailed, controllable image creation. The data and training pipeline develops these capabilities together. knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary and large-scale clustering guide semantic coverage, while bilingual captions, verified editing pairs, and training-time feedback improve the relevance and quality of supervision. Progressive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning extend the model to native 1.5K resolution. Task-specific reinforcement learning then refines generation and editing, and noise-aware on-policy distillation brings their specialized capabilities back into one checkpoint. This combines joint learning across tasks with targeted optimization of their distinct quality requirements. The reported evaluations demonstrate strong performance in bilingual generation, text rendering, image editing, and multi-reference composition, including leading overall results among the evaluated open-source baselines on PRISMBench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench. Few-step distillation extends this model family to eﬀicient deployment: WeLM-Image-Turbo supports generation and editing with eight guidance-free steps and generates 1024 1024 image in 4.98 on single NVIDIA H20 GPU. Together with these results, the model, data pipeline, and training methodology provide practical foundation for high-quality image creation in WeChats consumer services. Further work will focus on stronger visual reasoning, more reliable control under complex instructions, and continued improvements in eﬀiciency.
